items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Enzymes don't 'fit' substrates — they fit transition states
items.claim: The textbook 'lock and key' model says enzymes have an active site that matches the substrate. Real enzymes are much more interesting: they bind the TRANSITION STATE of the reaction more tightly than the substrate or product.
items.prompt: Why does binding the transition state make a better catalyst?

options.text: It doesn't matter what the enzyme binds tightly
Stabilising the highest-energy point in the reaction lowers the activation energy; an enzyme that binds the transition state by 1000-fold relative to substrate accelerates the reaction by 1000-fold
Binding the substrate tightly always speeds up reactions
The substrate spontaneously becomes the transition state

items.reveal_title: Linus Pauling's prediction and modern enzyme design
items.reveal:
Pauling proposed in 1948 that enzymes catalyse reactions by binding most strongly to the transition state, lowering the activation energy.

Direct evidence: 'transition state analogues' — stable molecules that mimic the transition state's geometry — bind enzymes 10 to 10,000 times more tightly than the substrates themselves. Many drugs are designed this way (statins like atorvastatin mimic the transition state of HMG-CoA reductase).

Catalytic antibodies, raised against transition state analogues, can catalyse reactions for which no natural enzyme exists (Schultz, Lerner, 1986). De novo enzyme design (Baker lab, 2008 onward) explicitly engineers active sites to fit predicted transition states.

The induced-fit model (Koshland 1958) and the transition-state model are both refinements of the original lock-and-key.
items.why: Lock-and-key implies stable binding of stable molecules. Enzymes catalyse by binding unstable, fleeting transition states — a much subtler picture.

items.title: Eyes have evolved independently more than 40 times
items.claim: Eyes are complicated. Darwin worried about them in Origin of Species. Modern phylogenetics shows that eyes — from basic photoreceptors to full image-forming structures — have evolved independently somewhere between 40 and 60 times across animal lineages.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about evolution?

options.text: Eyes are too complex to evolve once, let alone many times

Photoreception is selected for so strongly that wherever a workable starting point exists (a light-sensitive protein) selection assembles eyes; complex outcomes evolve repeatedly when the gradient of advantage is steep
All eyes descend from a single ancestor
Vision is impossible without divine design

items.reveal_title: Eyes as evolutionary stress-tests for gradualism
items.reveal:
Modern eyes include: vertebrate camera eyes, cephalopod camera eyes (independently evolved, no blind spot), trilobite calcite-lens compound eyes, scallop mirror eyes, copepod parabolic-reflector eyes, jumping-spider sharp-focus eyes, brittle-star whole-body lensed skin.

Nilsson and Pelger (1994) modelled the evolution of a vertebrate-style camera eye from a flat patch of photoreceptors. With realistic mutation rates and selection coefficients of 1 percent, they estimated 400,000 generations — about half a million years — to produce a fully functional eye.

The common element across all 40+ origins: opsin proteins. The receptor molecules are conserved; the architectures around them have been built and rebuilt many times.
items.why: Eyes feel like such complex organs that they 'must' be hard to evolve. They are exactly the kind of thing selection invents many times when given a good starting molecule.
